cover.howToUse: Fill in each blank while its slide is up. Record the important items, not every word. The last line of each block is the slide's example.

sectionsContent.title: Why Periodic Trends Change
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can explain periodic trends using protons, energy levels, and shielding.

notes.answer: A period is a row. A group is a column.

notes.prompt: Across a row, atoms gain more
notes.answer: protons, so the outer electrons are pulled inward

notes.prompt: Down a group, atoms gain another
notes.answer: energy level
Inner electrons reduce the pull felt by outer electrons.

notes.prompt: Example: Li vs. F, Li vs. Na
notes.answer: Li 3 protons, F 9 protons. Li 2 levels, Na 3 levels.

sectionsContent.title: Ionization Energy & Electronegativity
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe and explain the trends in ionization energy and electronegativity.

notes.answer: Energy needed to remove an electron from a gas atom (kJ/mol).
Generally increases across a row → and up a column ↑.
More nuclear pull = harder to remove. More distance and shielding = easier.

notes.prompt: Example: Ca vs. Br, higher ionization energy
notes.answer: Br. Same period; 15 more protons.
an inner electron was removed
3 (the jump is at the 4th)
2 (the jump is at the 3rd)
How strongly an atom pulls on shared electrons in a bond (no units).
Generally increases across a row → and up a column ↑. Fluorine is highest; noble gases excluded.
More nuclear pull attracts shared electrons. More distance and shielding weaken it.

notes.prompt: Example: rank S, O, F, lowest to highest
notes.answer: S < O < F

sectionsContent.title: Atomic & Ionic Radius
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe and explain the atomic radius trend and compare an ion to its atom.

notes.answer: The size of an atom (pm).
Generally increases down a column ↓ and to the left across a row ←.
Down: another energy level adds size. Across: more protons pull electrons inward.

notes.prompt: Example: Ca vs. Br, larger atom
notes.answer: Ca. Same period; Br has more protons pulling inward.
The ion is smaller: 12 electrons → 10 electrons.
The outer level is gone. The nucleus still has 12 protons.

sectionsContent.title: Melting & Boiling Points; Trend Summary
sectionsContent.learningTarget: I can describe the melting and boiling point patterns in groups 1 and 17 and summarize the periodic trends.

notes.answer: Melting: solid → liquid. Boiling: liquid → gas. Both in °C.
No single trend. Down group 1 both fall (Li → Cs); down group 17 both rise (F → I).
Stronger attractions need more energy to overcome. Different bonds give different patterns.

notes.prompt: Example: group 17, highest melting and boiling point
notes.answer: Iodine, I₂ (113.7 °C, 184.4 °C): larger molecules attract more strongly.
Higher ionization energy, higher electronegativity
Larger atomic radius, stronger metallic character
How easily an atom loses electrons; strong near Cs.
